newsitem.title: CHINA: SOYBEAN PRICES HIGH, WEATHER VOLATILE FOR CHINA.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEAN PRICES HIGH, WEATHER VOLATILE FOR CHINA.

text.p: High prices and volatile weather are keeping China out of the soybean market, traders in Asia said on Friday.
Despite sharp falls on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) on Thursday, prices were still some $10 to $15 a tonne too high for serious Chinese buying interest, a trader in Singapore said.
CBOT soybean futures ended sharply lower on Thursday as funds sold amid bearish sentiment about the weather in growing areas, and crop output forecasts.
Soybeans ended 23-1/2 to 12 cents per bushel lower, with November down 21-1/2 at $6.28-1/2 and August off 23-1/2 at $7.45-1/2.
These seven to 10 days were crucial for soybeans, Asian traders said, echoing their CBOT colleagues.
Traders talked weather on Friday, saying that some houses were changing their minds by the hour according to the latest they had heard on weather patterns in the U.S. Midwest.
That volatility was a factor in the 120,000 tonnes of washouts of Chinese soybean orders, as well as 150,000 tonnes of soybean defaults, they said.

The washouts, however, worked to everybody's benefit, an Asian source said, "because in a market this volatile, every trader knows that if it rains, the market will collapse. In that environment what you want to do is get out of a contract".
"Washouts in China in most cases means you pay them, they never pay you," another trader said.
As prices rallied last week, before the subsequent dips, prices inclusive of cost and freight (c&f) would have been higher than the original selling price, he said.
Sellers fearing a drop below the selling price -- and the possibility that they would lose the difference -- offered to split the current difference with their buyers, he said.
With the seller having already hedged, and the buyer picking up a bonus for washing out, everybody was happy.
Prices on the soy complex had bounced up and down all week on weather, traders said, and with this weekend's outlook vital to pricing, Friday was guaranteed to be quiet.
"Asians are never good buyers in a falling market because they all want a bottom peg and there is no such thing," another Asian source said.
Likewise, he said, Asian were not good sellers in a rising market.
"What are you going to do on a Friday?" said another trader, adding that Project A volume was the lowest he had seen in 10 days.
"With the same weather forecast nobody wants to take positions, especially when the weekend weather is crucial," he said. "So on Monday we will see a lot of activity."

The market would remain quiet until bottoming out, traders said. This could see some interest from China, which would hit the CBOT and lead to a scurry of follow-up buying and a possible rally, they said.
"But you want to see that bottoming out first," said one traders. "It's a chicken-and-egg thing."
-- Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-7004
